messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 42

He is a 44-year-old South Asian man who comes to see the therapist carrying a life that has been divided into before and after. He speaks of his home country in careful pieces at first, as if the whole story might break him open if he tells it too quickly. Years ago, conflict overtakes the neighborhood where he lives. What begins as rumors in the street becomes soldiers, checkpoints, raids in the night, and the constant understanding that any ordinary errand can turn dangerous without warning. He is still young enough then to believe that if he stays useful, keeps his head down, and works hard, he can protect himself and the people around him. He is a chef even then, someone who knows how to feed others, how to keep a kitchen moving under pressure, how to make something warm and sustaining out of very little. That identity matters to him, because it gives him a role when everything else feels uncertain.

But the violence reaches him anyway. He loses neighbors, then friends, and eventually the sense that home is a place that can hold him. He describes the moment he realizes he must leave as both frantic and numb: bags packed too quickly, money hidden in his clothes, the taste of panic in his mouth, and the strange guilt of abandoning the people who cannot go with him. The journey into refugee life is marked by long waits, cold nights, and the humiliation of depending on strangers for safety. He learns to scan faces before speaking, to listen for the tone of authority, to hold his breath whenever a loud voice cuts through a room. Even now, years later, he remembers how often he was told to wait, to prove who he was, to stand in line, to move along. Being unprotected becomes its own kind of injury.

In the present, he lives alone and works long hours in a restaurant kitchen, where the heat, noise, and speed suit him in some ways because they leave little room for thought. He is known as reliable, precise, and quiet. He can break down a fish in minutes, time a sauce by instinct, and keep working when others are overwhelmed. Yet the same environment also keeps him on edge. A pan dropped too hard can make his shoulders jerk. A shouted order across the kitchen can send a quick surge through his body, as if something worse is about to happen. He hates standing with his back to the door, and he notices exits wherever he goes. He arranges his life so that he can see who is coming into a room. He says he does this without thinking, but it has become automatic, part of the way he moves through the world.

At night, when the restaurant closes and the silence arrives, the old images come back with more force. He dreams of running through streets he can no longer trust, of carrying what he can while the rest is left behind. He wakes with his heart pounding, disoriented, sometimes reaching for the light before he knows where he is. Sleep feels shallow and easily broken. He often gets up and checks the locks, then checks them again. He tells himself he is being sensible, yet he also knows the ritual does not calm him for long. There is a tightness in him that does not fully leave. He startles easily. He finds himself irritable with coworkers when they crowd him or repeat instructions too sharply, then later feels ashamed of how quickly his temper rises. In quieter moments he feels detached, as though he is watching his own life from a distance.

He does not talk much about sadness, but it shows in how he has narrowed his world. He has no partner and says he has never had the patience to explain himself to someone who did not already understand loss. He keeps most relationships surface-level, careful not to become dependent. He avoids news coverage of war or refugee crises, though he may stop briefly when he catches a story, unable to look away even as it unsettles him. He lives with a persistent sense that danger can return without warning, and he measures safety in small, practical ways: a clear sightline, a familiar route home, a kitchen that functions the way it should. What stands out most is how much energy he spends staying composed. Underneath that composure is a man who has learned to survive by never fully relaxing, still carrying the memory of what it cost him to leave everything behind.
